title: How to Keep Syncee Price and Stock Sync from Drifting
excerpt: Price and stock drift quietly eats margin in a supplier marketplace store. Here is a weekly routine, a margin floor, and a set of failure rules that keep a synced catalog honest.
body: A marketplace catalog rarely fails all at once. It drifts. A supplier nudges a wholesale price up, a size goes out of stock for nine days, a variant quietly disappears, and your store keeps advertising a product at a margin that no longer exists. Automated syncing copies whatever the feed says, but it does not decide whether the new number is safe to sell at. That gap is where margin leaks in a Syncee store, and closing it takes a monitoring routine rather than a one-time setup.

Treat price and availability as two separate problems. Price drift is slow: a two dollar increase on a forty dollar item can turn a healthy product into a break-even one, especially once payment fees and shipping are included. Availability drift is loud but damaging, because a best seller that shows in stock in your storefront while the supplier has none generates refunds, support tickets, and ad spend on traffic that cannot convert. Each one needs its own threshold and its own response.

Set a landed margin floor before you monitor anything. For every listed product write down the wholesale cost, the shipping cost to your main market, the payment fee percentage, and your target margin, then compute the minimum retail price that still clears the floor. When a supplier feed pushes cost up, the question is no longer whether the price changed but whether the product still clears the floor. If it does not, you either reprice within the hour or pause the listing. Anything else means selling at a loss while the feed looks perfectly healthy.

Build a weekly review pass around the products that carry the most risk. Sort your catalog by ad spend and by order volume, check the top twenty every week, and work through the rest once a month. For each product confirm three things: the retail price still clears the margin floor, the supplier stock level matches what your storefront displays, and every variant you sell still exists on the supplier side. Twenty products takes about fifteen minutes once the numbers live in a sheet, and it catches nearly every expensive error before it compounds.

Give yourself written rules for what happens when a check fails. A product that dips below the floor comes out of advertising but stays live for organic traffic until you reprice it. A product whose supplier stock hits zero gets hidden rather than left to oversell, because an order you cannot fulfil costs more in support time than the sale is worth. A product that fails two consecutive checks gets removed instead of lingering as a dead listing that drags down collection quality. Rules remove the daily judgement calls that teams postpone.

The last piece is a change log. Every time you override a synced price or hide a product, record the date, the old number, and the reason. After a quarter you will see which suppliers drift most, which categories are volatile, and whether your floors are realistic. That history turns a reactive chore into a sourcing decision: drifting suppliers get replaced, stable ones get more shelf space.
